theme: Enter not into judgment with your servant
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 143. It is the last of the penitential psalms. Paul alludes to verse 2 in Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16. Notice the combination of confession, longing, and request for guidance.
settingTheScene: Psalm 143 is a prayer of David, perhaps from the time when Absalom pursued him. The enemy is real, but the deeper problem is that David knows that he cannot stand on his own merit before God. Verse 2 is the key line, and Paul used it to prove that no one is justified by works. With Psalms 32 and 130, it completes a trio on the theme of coming to God as a sinner.
observation: “Hear my prayer, O LORD; give ear to my pleas for mercy! In your faithfulness answer me, in your righteousness!” (v. 1).
“Enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you” (v. 2).
“Therefore my spirit faints within me; my heart within me is appalled” (v. 4).
“I remember the days of old; I meditate on all that you have done; I ponder the work of your hands” (v. 5).
“I stretch out my hands to you; my soul thirsts for you like a parched land” (v. 6).
“Let me hear in the morning of your steadfast love, for in you I trust” (v. 8).
“Teach me to do your will, for you are my God! Let your good Spirit lead me on level ground!” (v. 10).
“For your name’s sake, O LORD, preserve my life! In your righteousness bring my soul out of trouble!” (v. 11).
interpretation:
David opens by appealing to God’s faithfulness and righteousness. This is unusual. Normally one might expect him to appeal to his own innocence. Instead he appeals to God’s character. He is asking God to act in keeping with his own promises. And then the line that Paul loves: “Enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you.” David does not argue his case. He asks God not to bring him to court, because he would lose. This is the prayer of a man who understands that he is not righteous in himself. It is close to the cry of Romans 3.

The enemy has crushed David’s life to the ground, and he sits in darkness like those long dead. His spirit faints and his heart is appalled. This is an honest picture of despair, and the Bible does not hide it. What does David do? He remembers. “I remember the days of old; I meditate on all that you have done; I ponder the work of your hands.” When the present is dark, he looks at what God has done in the past. For Christians, the great work to remember is the cross and the resurrection.

He stretches out his hands, and his soul thirsts for God like parched land. Verses 7 to 10 are a series of brief requests: answer me quickly; let me hear of your steadfast love in the morning; make me know the way I should go; deliver me; teach me to do your will. Notice the order. First he asks to hear of God’s love, and then for guidance. We cannot follow God’s will without first resting in his love. And the prayer, “Let your good Spirit lead me on level ground,” anticipates the Spirit’s guidance for the believer.

The final plea rests on God’s name: “For your name’s sake, O LORD, preserve my life! In your righteousness bring my soul out of trouble.” David does not ask because he deserves it, but for the sake of God’s glory. In the end, he asks God to cut off his enemies, “for I am your servant.” The psalm ends with confidence in the relationship, not in himself.

How does this prepare us for Romans 5? We have just learned that no living person is righteous before God. The answer to David’s fear is the gospel: in Christ, God does enter into judgment, but he enters it on our behalf. The Judge himself has stood in the dock in our place.
connection: Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16 allude to verse 2. Psalm 51 and Psalm 130 are related. Job 9:2 and 25:4 also ask how a man can be righteous before God. Psalm 77:11-12 also speaks of remembering God’s works. Psalm 63:1 is another thirst psalm. Romans 8:14 says all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. Nehemiah 9:20 says God gave his good Spirit to instruct. Hebrews 4:15-16 says we have a high priest who sympathizes with our weakness.
application:
Remember specific works of God in your life. Write down three.

Pray verse 8 tomorrow morning, before checking your phone: let me hear of your steadfast love.

Ask the Spirit to lead you on level ground, and listen for his answer.
prayerPrompts: Ask God not to enter into judgment with you, since no one living is righteous.
Ask him to teach you to do his will.
Ask him to lead you on level ground.
